snip.t: Immune cells in lung – alveolar macrophages, neutrophils, complement: Rapid neutrophil influx creates purulent exudate; failure of opsonisation (e.g., splenic dysfunction) predisposes to encapsulated organisms like *Streptococcus pneumoniae*.
CAP: Streptococcus pneumoniae (commonest), *Haemophilus influenzae*, *Mycoplasma pneumoniae*, *Legionella*, *Chlamydophila*, viruses (influenza, RSV, SARS-CoV-2)
Community-acquired (Adults): *Streptococcus pneumoniae*, *Neisseria meningitidis* — *Herpes simplex virus-1 (HSV-1)*, Cerebral malaria
Basilar skull fracture / Post-trauma: *Streptococcus pneumoniae*, *Staphylococcus aureus* — Rabies virus (animal bite history)
Sputum Gram stain & culture: Lower respiratory pathogens — Gram‑positive cocci in chains → Streptococcus pneumoniae; Gram‑negative rods → H. influenzae, Klebsiella
Definitive therapy once culture/diagnostic results return; de‑escalate to narrow‑spectrum agents (e.g., amoxicillin for susceptible Streptococcus pneumoniae).

qs.q: A male infant is born at term with no congenital anomalies noted. A year later he has failure to thrive and has had one bacterial pneumonia after another, with both *Haemophilus influenzae* and *Streptococcus pneumoniae* cultured from sputum. Which disease is he most likely to have?
qs.e: * Recurrent bacterial infections suggest impaired B-cell function with lack of immunoglobulin production. Once protective maternal antibodies wane, the disease manifests more severely.
qs.s: Immunopathology MCQs — Source Paper Awaiting Edit

qs.q: A 62-year-old man has 3 months of dull back pain and develops a productive cough. CXR of the spine shows several 1–2 cm lytic vertebral lesions. Labs show BUN 49, creatinine 5, total protein 8.3, albumin 3.7. Sputum grows Streptococcus pneumoniae. Most likely bone marrow biopsy finding?
o: Presence of numerous malignant plasma cells
qs.e: Lytic bone lesions + renal failure + high total protein + recurrent encapsulated bacterial infections = multiple myeloma. Bone marrow shows sheets of plasma cells producing the abnormal immunoglobulin.

qs.q: Streptococcus pneumoniae can be normal flora in 5-40% of people. At what anatomic site?
qs.e: S. pneumoniae commonly colonizes the nasopharynx asymptomatically. Colonization rates are highest in children and can lead to invasive disease under certain conditions.

qs.q: Streptococcus pneumoniae is the most common cause of community-acquired bacterial meningitis in adults.
qs.e: While Neisseria meningitidis and Haemophilus influenzae type b are significant causes of bacterial meningitis, Streptococcus pneumoniae is considered the leading cause of bacterial meningitis in adults in many parts of the world, particularly in developed countries.

qs.q: Streptococcus pneumoniae is the most common cause of 'typical' pneumonia.
qs.e: Streptococcus pneumoniae is widely recognized as the most frequent bacterial cause of community-acquired pneumonia, often referred to as 'typical' pneumonia due to its characteristic presentation.
qs.s: Weekly Year 2: Microbiology Exam - June 12, 2026 (Section A: MCQs)

qs.q: The most common cause of acute bacterial meningitis in adults is Streptococcus pneumoniae.
qs.e: In adults, Streptococcus pneumoniae is the leading cause of community-acquired bacterial meningitis. While Neisseria meningitidis and Haemophilus influenzae are also significant pathogens, S. pneumoniae is generally considered the most common in this age group.

ai.subject: Microbiology & immunology
ai.summary: Streptococcus pneumoniae is a lancet‑shaped, alpha‑hemolytic bacterium that colonises the nasopharynx and can cause invasive disease when host defenses falter. It is the leading cause of community‑acquired pneumonia, meningitis and otitis media worldwide.

sections.p: A gram‑positive, encapsulated, alpha‑hemolytic coccus that thrives in the human upper respiratory tract. Its polysaccharide capsule is the main virulence factor, preventing phagocytosis and enabling invasive disease.
The capsule, pneumolysin, and autolysin are key virulence determinants. Antigenic diversity of the capsule (over 90 serotypes) complicates immunity and vaccine design.

Person‑to‑person spread via respiratory droplets. Colonisation is common in children; most adults are asymptomatic carriers. Stress, viral infection, or immunosuppression can trigger invasive disease.
Community‑acquired pneumonia (CAP), meningitis, otitis media, sinusitis, and bacteremia. Invasive disease is more likely in young children, the elderly, and immunocompromised hosts.
b: CAP: cough, fever, pleuritic chest pain
Meningitis: neck stiffness, altered mental status
Otitis media: ear pain, hearing loss

sections.p: Clinical suspicion plus rapid tests and cultures. Key investigations include chest X‑ray, blood cultures, sputum Gram stain, and urinary antigen test. In low‑resource settings, a rapid antigen test and basic imaging may suffice.

t.b: Detects pneumococcal C‑polysaccharide; positive suggests invasive disease; false negatives in early infection
Confirms bacteremia; low yield in CAP but critical in meningitis
Shows lancet‑shaped gram‑positive cocci in pairs; indicates pneumococcal pneumonia
Useful for carrier detection; low specificity in adults

sections.p: First‑line therapy is a beta‑lactam (e.g., amoxicillin) unless resistance is suspected. In severe or high‑risk cases, a third‑generation cephalosporin or a macrolide is added. Vaccination with PCV13 and PPSV23 reduces disease burden.

t.b: Guides beta‑lactam choice; high MIC indicates resistance
Determines vaccine effectiveness; low coverage may need broader vaccine

sections.p: Remember that pneumococcus is the most common cause of CAP and that its capsule is the main virulence factor. In low‑resource settings, a positive urinary antigen test can guide therapy when cultures are unavailable.

whenToSeekHelp: Severe dyspnea, confusion, high fever >39°C, chest pain not improving, signs of meningitis (neck stiffness, photophobia)

faq.a: It prevents phagocytosis, allowing the bacteria to survive in blood and cause invasive disease.

faq.q: Can a child with a normal chest X‑ray still have pneumococcal pneumonia?
faq.a: Yes, early infection may show subtle changes; clinical judgment and rapid tests guide treatment.

faq.q: What if the patient is allergic to penicillin?
faq.a: Use a macrolide or doxycycline if no resistance; consider a cephalosporin if allergy is not severe.
